hints: Look at the electron micrograph - find the fluid-filled central region enclosed by the inner membrane, not the folded membranes themselves.
walkthrough:
Picture the Mitochondrion in 3D**
Think of the mitochondrion as having two membranes. The outer membrane is smooth, the inner membrane is folded. The large fluid space inside the inner membrane is the matrix.

Link Compartment to Stage of Respiration**
The Krebs cycle is catalysed by soluble enzymes dissolved in aqueous solution, so it occurs in the matrix. Glycolysis is in the cytoplasm and oxidative phosphorylation is on the inner membrane, so A must point to the central matrix area.
Final answer: Label A with line to the mitochondrial matrix (the central aqueous compartment).

hints: Label B points to one of the finger-like folds projecting into the centre - recall the special name given to folds of the inner membrane.
walkthrough:
Read What B Points To**
B is pointing to one of the dark shelf-like folds that project from the edge into the middle of the mitochondrion. These are all continuous with the inner membrane.

Recall the Correct Term**
Folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane are called cristae (singular: crista). They greatly increase the area available for oxidative phosphorylation.
Final answer: Crista (cristae).

hints: Start with the shape you see in Fig. 8.1 - what does folding do to the available area for membrane proteins?
Think about which two types of protein complexes must be housed in this membrane for oxidative phosphorylation.
Consider why the membrane must prevent protons leaking back except through one route.
Link proton pumping to the intermembrane space and the concentration difference created.
Check you have paired each structural feature with its functional benefit, not just listed structures.
walkthrough:
Folding Gives Large Surface Area**
The inner membrane is folded into many cristae. This creates a very large surface area in a small volume, so many electron carriers of the electron transport chain and many ATP synthase complexes can be embedded.

Housing the Machinery for Oxidative Phosphorylation**
Electrons from NADH and FADH2 pass along electron carriers and cytochromes in the membrane, releasing energy. That energy is used by proton pumps to pump protons ($H^+$) from the matrix into the intermembrane space.

Keeping the Gradient for Chemiosmosis**
The inner membrane is impermeable to protons, so protons cannot diffuse back freely. This maintains a high concentration of protons in the intermembrane space - an electrochemical proton gradient. Protons then flow back only through ATP synthase, driving synthesis of ATP from ADP and Pi.

Final answer: Inner membrane is highly folded into cristae giving large surface area for electron transport chain carriers/cytochromes and ATP synthase; membrane contains proton pumps and is impermeable to protons, allowing build-up of high proton concentration in intermembrane space to form proton gradient for chemiosmosis and ATP synthesis.

hints: Recall the blue redox dyes used in respiration experiments that accept electrons in place of the normal acceptor.
Think about what happens to the colour of that dye when it gains the electrons released in Fig. 8.2.
walkthrough:
Name a Suitable Redox Dye**
DCPIP or methylene blue are blue in the oxidised state and can act as artificial electron acceptors. They take up the electrons ($e^-$) shown being released as succinate is oxidised to fumarate.

Link Colour Change to Activity**
When reduced by gaining electrons, the dye changes from blue to colourless. The faster succinate dehydrogenase works, the faster electrons are released and the faster the blue colour disappears, so time to decolourise measures rate of respiration.

Final answer: DCPIP (or methylene blue); indicator is reduced by accepting electrons from succinate / succinate dehydrogenase, changing from blue to colourless, so rate of colour change measures enzyme activity.

hints: First follow each curve from left to right - how does rate change as succinate rises from 0 to about $1.0 \text{mmol dm}^{-3}$ and after?
Now compare like with like for temperature - pick liver at $37 ^\circ\text{C}$ versus liver at $10 ^\circ\text{C}$, and muscle versus muscle.
Finally compare tissues at the same temperature and add numbers from the y-axis to support your statements.
walkthrough:
Describe the Substrate Effect**
All four curves rise steeply at low succinate concentration then level off. Maximum rate is reached by about $1.0 \text{mmol dm}^{-3}$ succinate, after which adding more substrate has little effect as enzyme becomes saturated.

Compare Temperatures and Tissues**
At any succinate concentration, the $37 ^\circ\text{C}$ curves are much higher than the $10 ^\circ\text{C}$ curves. And muscle is always above liver at the same temperature. For example, plateau at about 210 arbitrary units for muscle at $37 ^\circ\text{C}$ compared to about 100 for liver at $37 ^\circ\text{C}$, while at $10 ^\circ\text{C}$ muscle plateaus at about 25 and liver at about 10.

Keep Description Separate from Explanation**
Here you only need trends and numbers with units. Do not explain why yet - that comes in (ii). Always quote comparative data to earn full credit.

Final answer: Rate increases with succinate up to approx $1.0 \text{mmol dm}^{-3}$ then plateaus; rate higher at $37 ^\circ\text{C}$ than at $10 ^\circ\text{C}$; rate higher in muscle than liver at both temperatures, e.g. max approx 210 arbitrary units for muscle at $37 ^\circ\text{C}$ vs approx 100 for liver at $37 ^\circ\text{C}$ vs approx 25 and 10 at $10 ^\circ\text{C}$.

hints: What is the useful product of respiration that muscle cells need in large amounts?
Think about what muscle does that liver does not do continuously - what process uses that product directly?
Link higher ATP need to higher respiration rate and more mitochondria or enzyme activity in muscle.
walkthrough:
Start from the Purpose of Respiration**
Aerobic respiration releases energy to make ATP. The rate of respiration therefore matches the demand for ATP.

Contrast Muscle and Liver Work**
Skeletal muscle contracts for movement, posture and shivering, which hydrolyses large amounts of ATP by myosin ATPase and ion pumps. Liver is metabolically active but does not contract, so its ATP demand per unit mass is lower.

Conclude the Causal Chain**
Higher ATP demand in muscle selects for higher succinate dehydrogenase activity and higher respiration rate, giving the higher curves in Fig. 8.4 at $37 ^\circ\text{C}$. This is not that muscle tries to respire faster, it is that more ATP use requires more ATP production.

Final answer: Respiration produces ATP; muscle has higher ATP / energy demand than liver for muscle contraction / because muscle is more metabolically active, e.g. for movement and shivering to maintain body temperature, so higher rate of respiration.

hints: Even when curled up asleep at $10 ^\circ\text{C}$, which tissue still maintains some tension or heat production to protect the animal?
walkthrough:
Think About Torpor Survival**
In torpor the squirrel is curled in a sphere underground at $10 ^\circ\text{C}$. Liver metabolism can fall very low, but muscle must maintain some tone and can shiver or generate heat to allow arousal to euthermia.

Give the One Reason**
Because muscle stays partly contracted and more metabolically active to generate heat, it still uses more energy than liver tissue during torpor.
Final answer: Muscle remains contracted / maintains muscle tone / generates heat / is more metabolically active than liver during torpor.
